Frontier LLMs can navigate complex websites, but their cost and reliance on third-party APIs make local deployment impractical. We introduce Agent-as-Annotators, a framework that structures synthetic trajectory generation for web agents by analogy to human annotation roles, replacing the Task Designer, Annotator, and Supervisor with modular LLM components. Using Gemini 3 Pro as teacher, we generate 3,000 trajectories across six web environments and fine-tune a 9B-parameter student with pure supervised learning on the 2,322 that pass quality filtering. The resulting model achieves 41.5% on WebArena, surpassing closed-source models such as Claude 3.5 Sonnet (36.0%) and GPT-4o (31.5%) under the same evaluation protocol, and nearly doubling the previous best open-weight result (Go-Browse, 21.7%). Capabilities transfer to unseen environments, with an 18.2 percentage point gain on WorkArena L1 (an enterprise platform never seen during training) and consistent improvements across three additional benchmarks. Ablations confirm that each pipeline component contributes meaningfully, with Judge filtering, evaluation hints, and reasoning traces each accounting for measurable gains. These results demonstrate that structured trajectory synthesis from a single frontier teacher is sufficient to produce competitive, locally deployable web agents. Project page: https://agent-as-annotators.github.io

The relationships between teachers and students are essential to quality education. As A.I. is more and more woven into educational practice, these relationships are being configured in ways that go beyond efficiency of instruction. Examine how AI-mediated educational environments influence the trust, dialogue, and human bonding targets of teacher-student relationships in the AI era. Through the lens of relational and ethical theories of education, AI is conceptualized as a sociotechnical mediator rather than a neutral/moral agent. The examination illustrates that algorithmic authority can destroy relational trust while the simulated interaction obscures the ethical grounding of pedagogical dialogue and over-automation threatens the loss of emotional presence and care. In response, the research forwards a human-centered relational framework that situates AI as an augmentative aid supporting rather than supplanting human judgment, dialogic engagement, and human bonding, and outlines implications for practice, teacher education, and policy.

Existing accountability frameworks for AI systems, legal, ethical, and regulatory, rest on a shared assumption: for any consequential outcome, at least one identifiable person had enough involvement and foresight to bear meaningful responsibility. This paper proves that agentic AI systems violate this assumption not as an engineering limitation but as a mathematical necessity once autonomy exceeds a computable threshold. We introduce Human-Agent Collectives, a formalisation of joint human-AI systems where agents are modelled as state-policy tuples within a shared structural causal model. Autonomy is characterised through a four-dimensional information-theoretic profile (epistemic, executive, evaluative, social); collective behaviour through interaction graphs and joint action spaces. We axiomatise legitimate accountability through four minimal properties: Attributability (responsibility requires causal contribution), Foreseeability Bound (responsibility cannot exceed predictive capacity), Non-Vacuity (at least one agent bears non-trivial responsibility), and Completeness (all responsibility must be fully allocated). Our central result, the Accountability Incompleteness Theorem, proves that for any collective whose compound autonomy exceeds the Accountability Horizon and whose interaction graph contains a human-AI feedback cycle, no framework can satisfy all four properties simultaneously. The impossibility is structural: transparency, audits, and oversight cannot resolve it without reducing autonomy. Below the threshold, legitimate frameworks exist, establishing a sharp phase transition. Experiments on 3,000 synthetic collectives confirm all predictions with zero violations. This is the first impossibility result in AI governance, establishing a formal boundary below which current paradigms remain valid and above which distributed accountability mechanisms become necessary.

documents.abstract: The history of human civilization has been shaped by war, each conflict etching its legacy into the fabric of existence. Yet, what if the final war, the one that concludes the saga of humanity, is upon us? In this thought-provoking exploration, Prof. Dr. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad, Ph.D., DBA, delves into the philosophical, ethical, and existential implications of humanity’s last war. This book does not merely examine warfare as a strategic or political tool but questions its role in defining human identity. As technological advancements in weaponry accelerate toward an uncontrollable abyss, the line between self-defense and self-destruction blurs. From the ethical dilemmas of nuclear warfare to the digital battlegrounds of the future, every chapter illuminates the fragility of peace and the looming shadow of extinction. By weaving historical analysis, philosophical reflections, and contemporary case studies, this work serves as both a warning and an inquiry. Can war be averted, or is it an inevitable conclusion to human nature? What moral responsibilities do global leaders bear in preventing such devastation? With deep intellectual rigor and an urgent sense of realism, this book invites readers to confront the possibility of the last war—not as a distant nightmare but as a stark reality demanding immediate contemplation. The writing of this book is deeply rooted in the concern that modern warfare has evolved beyond conventional understanding. Prof. Dr. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad, Ph.D., DBA, authored this work in response to the alarming trajectory of global conflicts that now intertwine with technological singularity, artificial intelligence, and weapons of unprecedented destruction. Published in 2011, this study aims to dissect the philosophical dimensions of war, highlighting the paradox of progress that brings humanity closer to its ultimate demise. War has long been perceived as a mechanism of power, control, and territorial expansion. However, this book redefines conflict not as an isolated event but as a culmination of human ideologies, fears, and the relentless pursuit of superiority. The discussion extends beyond conventional military strategies, touching upon cyberwarfare, biological weapons, and AI-driven conflicts, emphasizing the urgency of ethical governance over technological advancements. The rapid militarization of space, the increasing automation of warfare, and the unpredictable nature of geopolitical tensions have necessitated a deeper inquiry into the finality of war. Prof. Dr. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad, Ph.D., DBA, observed that humanity stands at a critical threshold where the distinction between war and annihilation is vanishing. The rise of unmanned combat systems and autonomous decision-making weapons amplifies the risk of irreversible global catastrophe. The central theme of this book is the philosophical interrogation of war's necessity and its ethical ramifications. Through existentialist and utilitarian perspectives, the book scrutinizes whether human civilization can exist without conflict or if war is embedded in the very essence of human survival. The exploration is not limited to military confrontations but extends to socio-political conflicts, ideological warfare, and economic battles that shape global stability. While wars of the past have followed discernible patterns, modern warfare presents unpredictability fueled by technological dominance. The book identifies economic disparity, resource depletion, and political radicalization as harbingers of the last war. These indicators serve as a warning system for humanity, urging proactive measures before irreversible escalation. Prof. Dr. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad, Ph.D., DBA, establishes multiple variables essential for understanding war’s trajectory, including state sovereignty, military-industrial expansion, ethical considerations in AI warfare, and the psychological conditioning of societies toward conflict acceptance. By analyzing these elements, the book constructs a framework to predict and possibly mitigate future large-scale wars. Several key factors drive the discussion within this book: the historical repetition of wars despite peace efforts, the weaponization of emerging technologies, and the philosophical dilemma of whether war is an unavoidable consequence of civilization. The study also considers the role of global governance institutions and their effectiveness in preventing mass destruction. The work presents theoretical and practical approaches to conflict resolution, advocating for diplomatic restructuring, ethical AI governance, and alternative frameworks for international negotiations. Prof. Dr. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad, Ph.D., DBA, proposes a shift in global priorities—from military investment to sustainable human development—as a critical strategy in averting global catastrophe. The path toward eradicating war is fraught with challenges, including political resistance, economic dependencies on warfare industries, and the psychological normalization of conflict. While international organizations and peace movements provide counterbalances, the overwhelming momentum of military expansion presents a formidable obstacle to lasting peace. In summarizing the philosophical inquiry into the last war, this book serves as a stark reminder of the fragility of civilization. It posits that the final war is not an abstract fear but a plausible outcome if humanity fails to reassess its approach to power, aggression, and technological development. Through this reflective journey, Prof. Dr. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad, Ph.D., DBA, urges leaders, thinkers, and global citizens to engage in deeper discourse on the ethical and existential stakes of continued warfare.

Prosocial behavior is crucial for the development of adolescents. Prosocial behavior requires strong internal motivation to drive it, but the prospective association between the two is still unclear. In addition, there is still a gap in the relationship between grade motivation as a unique external motivation and prosocial behavior. To explore the prospective associations between them, we conducted two follow-up surveys (six months apart) on 862 Chinese adolescents (423 boys and 439 girls) to collect data on intrinsic motivation, grade motivation and prosocial behavior (relational prosocial behavior and practical prosocial behavior). The cross-lagged panel study results revealed that intrinsic motivation at T1 was positively associated with relational and practical prosocial behavior at T2. In contrast, grade motivation at T1 was not significantly associated with later prosocial behavior, and prosocial behavior at T1 was not significantly associated with later intrinsic motivation or grade motivation. These findings indicate that intrinsic motivation may be a potential antecedent for prosocial behavior in Chinese adolescents later in life, but the observed associations should be cautiously interpreted.
topics: Child and Adolescent Psychosocial and Emotional Development

documents.abstract: This study investigated the moderating role of gender and generational cohorts on the effects of artificial intelligence (AI) usage, learning adaptability, and academic performance of university students in Zimbabwe. Three hundred and twenty-five students at Great Zimbabwe University, Zimbabwe Open University and Women's University in Africa responded to the questionnaires. The study found that AI usage and learning adaptability positively effect academic performance. The study found that generational cohort moderates the effects of AI usage on academic performance, but gender does not. The findings of this research are that gender and generational cohort do not moderate the effects of learning adaptability and academic performance of university students in Zimbabwe. The research implies that students should use AI to enhance their academic performance and develop learning adaptability, which is also key to academic performance.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Multimodal learning is an emerging research topic across multiple disciplines but has rarely been applied to planetary science. In this contribution, we propose a single, unified transformer architecture trained to learn shared representations between multiple sources like grayscale images, Digital Elevation Models (DEMs), surface normals, and albedo maps. The architecture supports flexible translation from any input modality to any target modality. Our results demonstrate that our foundation model learns physically plausible relations across these four modalities. We further identify that image-based 3D reconstruction and albedo estimation (Shape and Albedo from Shading) of lunar images can be formulated as a multimodal learning problem. Our results demonstrate the potential of multimodal learning to solve Shape and Albedo from Shading and provide a new approach for large-scale planetary 3D reconstruction. Adding more input modalities in the future will further improve the results and enable tasks such as photometric normalization and co-registration.

The rapid expansion of irrigated fruit production in the Petrolina–Juazeiro hub has positioned the Brazilian semiarid as a strategic agro-export region, while simultaneously intensifying socioenvironmental inequalities and occupational health risks. This paradox reflects a development model in which economic gains coexist with diffuse and often invisible forms of exposure. This study aims to analyze the socioenvironmental and health impacts associated with irrigated agribusiness, focusing on the interaction between chemical exposure, water dynamics, and territorial vulnerability. An integrative literature review was conducted using international and regional databases, complemented by grey literature. A total of 216 records were initially identified and subjected to systematic screening and eligibility procedures. The analysis was structured around three axes: biochemical-clinical, socioeconomic, and geoenvironmental. The results indicate that pesticide exposure in the region is chronic, cumulative, and mediated by environmental and social factors. Evidence shows associations with genotoxicity, endocrine disruption, and underreported chronic diseases, alongside labor precariousness and gender inequality. Contamination pathways extend through soil and water systems, amplifying exposure beyond occupational settings. The discussion reveals that these dynamics are embedded in a broader framework of environmental injustice, where risks are unevenly distributed and structurally produced. The interaction between climate conditions, irrigation systems, and chemical use intensifies exposure, supporting the conceptualization of a chemical-hydric exposome. In conclusion, the study highlights the need for integrated regulatory approaches, improved surveillance systems, and policies that address cumulative exposure and territorial inequalities in semiarid agro-export regions.
topics: Effects and risks of endocrine disrupting chemicals

documents.abstract: War is not merely fought with weapons on the battlefield but is shaped long before the first shot is fired. 2011. The Political Philosophy of War Propaganda and Its Consequences is a profound exploration of how propaganda has been systematically used to manipulate perceptions, justify conflicts, and sustain power structures. Prof. Dr. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad, Ph.D., DBA, unveils the intricate relationship between war narratives, state agendas, and the psychological conditioning of societies. Published in 2011 in Geneva, Switzerland, this book critically examines the philosophy underpinning propaganda and its far-reaching implications. The pages unravel historical and contemporary examples of war propaganda, shedding light on how information is weaponized to manufacture consent. Governments, media, and international institutions are dissected as the architects of public opinion, often distorting reality to serve political and economic interests. The book further explores how the United Nations, as a global entity, struggles to navigate these deceptive narratives while attempting to maintain peace and diplomacy. Education is presented as both a battleground and a tool for resistance. The Education Training Centre is examined as a potential counterforce against the institutionalized manipulation of truth. By fostering critical thinking and ethical discourse, societies can reclaim their agency and dismantle the illusions that perpetuate endless cycles of war. This book is a wake-up call—an urgent appeal to question, analyze, and resist the forces that dictate the course of global conflict. The motivation for writing this book arises from the undeniable impact of propaganda in shaping wars and their aftermath. Prof. Dr. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad, Ph.D., DBA, seeks to unravel the mechanisms that allow propaganda to thrive and its role in constructing war as a necessary, even heroic, endeavor. The book was published in 2011 in Geneva, Switzerland, a city renowned for its diplomatic engagements and as a hub of international discourse on peace and conflict. History has repeatedly demonstrated that wars are not only fought with military power but also with narratives that legitimize aggression. From ancient empires to modern superpowers, states have mastered the art of persuasion to justify violence, rally populations, and silence opposition. This book challenges these accepted truths, urging readers to dissect the real motivations behind global conflicts. To understand the philosophy of war propaganda, Prof. Dr. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad, Ph.D., DBA, defines key concepts such as "manufactured consent," "psychological warfare," and "strategic misinformation." The book provides an analytical framework to decipher how propaganda functions across different political systems and historical periods. Truth becomes a malleable instrument in the hands of those who control information. The book dissects how linguistic framing, emotional appeal, and repetition are used to construct compelling war narratives that suppress critical thinking and pacify opposition. The modern world presents an evolution in propaganda techniques. Prof. Dr. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad, Ph.D., DBA, highlights the role of digital warfare, social media manipulation, and the emergence of artificial intelligence-driven disinformation campaigns. Governments and non-state actors alike now have unprecedented tools to shape perceptions on a global scale. Case studies illustrate how recent conflicts have been fueled by misinformation, fabricated threats, and the demonization of opponents. The book presents chilling examples of how media, once seen as a guardian of truth, often becomes complicit in amplifying war rhetoric. This book is built upon principles that deconstruct the political philosophy of propaganda. Prof. Dr. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad, Ph.D., DBA, adopts an interdisciplinary approach, integrating political science, psychology, and media studies to expose how war narratives are crafted and sustained. Through a comparative analysis of historical and contemporary conflicts, the book establishes a framework to recognize and challenge propaganda in real time. The goal is not just to understand the phenomenon but to empower individuals and institutions to resist its influence. To assess the presence and impact of war propaganda, this book identifies recurring indicators, including: • The deliberate distortion of facts to justify military action. • The portrayal of war as an act of moral duty or national survival. • The suppression of dissenting voices through censorship or intimidation. • The glorification of military actions while downplaying civilian casualties. Prof. Dr. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad, Ph.D., DBA, meticulously examines these elements, providing readers with analytical tools to recognize propaganda before it takes hold. The effectiveness of war propaganda is influenced by several operational variables, which include state control over media, public education, and ideological indoctrination. Prof. Dr. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad, Ph.D., DBA, reveals how these variables intersect to create a cohesive and persuasive narrative that discourages critical scrutiny. A crucial aspect of this analysis is the role of education as both a target and a solution. The book explores how school curricula, history books, and public discourse shape perceptions of war from an early age. The persistence of war propaganda is driven by key determinant factors such as: • The geopolitical interests of states seeking to expand influence. • The economic benefits of sustained military conflicts. • The ideological rivalries that create perpetual divisions. • The complicity of mass media in disseminating misleading information. Prof. Dr. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad, Ph.D., DBA, argues that these factors create a self-reinforcing system that ensures propaganda remains a powerful force in global politics. While propaganda is deeply entrenched in political structures, strategies exist to counter its effects. The book proposes reforms in education, media literacy programs, and international regulations on misinformation. Prof. Dr. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad, Ph.D., DBA, emphasizes the importance of academic institutions and global organizations in fostering a more informed and critically engaged society. The role of The Education Training Centre is examined as a model for institutions dedicated to cultivating critical thinking and resistance to manipulative narratives. Efforts to dismantle propaganda face resistance from state entities, corporate media interests, and political ideologues who benefit from maintaining control over information. Prof. Dr. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad, Ph.D., DBA, acknowledges these challenges while also highlighting the growing movement of independent journalism and grassroots educational initiatives pushing back against misinformation. The book closes with a sobering yet hopeful message. Prof. Dr. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad, Ph.D., DBA, asserts that propaganda will always exist, but its power depends on the willingness of societies to accept it without question. By cultivating skepticism, promoting transparency, and demanding accountability, humanity can reclaim its autonomy from those who seek to manipulate truth for political gain.

COVID-19 exposed structural fragilities in the United States' public health logistics and supply chain systems, particularly in the domains of diagnostic testing, epidemiological tracking, and coordinated response. These deficiencies underscore the urgent need for more adaptive, data-centric surveillance infrastructures capable of operating at scale and in real time. Artificial intelligence–enabled analytics, when integrated with existing public health systems, offer a viable pathway to enhance situational awareness, optimize resource allocation, and improve the timeliness of intervention strategies. In particular, wastewater-based epidemiology; augmented by AI-driven pattern recognition and predictive modeling; presents a scalable and cost-effective mechanism for population-level health monitoring, capable of detecting emerging threats prior to clinical reporting. This study advances that premise by examining how such integrative approaches can strengthen logistical decision-making and supply chain responsiveness.

documents.abstract: In teacher education contexts, developing foreign language communicative competence among non-language major students remains a persistent challenge, often characterized by low learning engagement, limited willingness to communicate, and weak transfer of classroom learning into actual communicative performance. Existing studies have predominantly focused on instructional methods or curriculum innovations, while relatively little attention has been paid to the underlying mechanisms through which foundational teaching conditions exert their influence on learners’ communicative development. Against this background, the present study investigates the mechanisms through which teaching foundations influence the development of foreign language communicative competence among nonlanguage major students in normal universities. Drawing on second language acquisition theory, educational psychology, and sociocultural perspectives, this study constructs an integrated analytical framework that links teaching foundations (including teacher support, classroom interaction design, curriculum structure, and assessment practices) with key mediating variables, namely learning engagement and willingness to communicate (WTC). Through systematic theoretical analysis and mechanism modeling, the study demonstrates that teaching foundations do not exert a direct and linear impact on communicative competence. Instead, their influence is primarily realized through a chain of mediating mechanisms. Specifically, supportive teaching foundations significantly enhance learners’ behavioral, emotional, and cognitive engagement, which in turn strengthens their willingness to communicate in the foreign language. Enhanced willingness to communicate subsequently promotes more frequent and higher-quality language use, thereby facilitating the development of communicative competence. Among the mediating variables, emotional engagement plays a particularly critical role in activating willingness to communicate, while curriculum structure and formative assessment exert stronger effects on cognitive engagement.

Tool learning has emerged as a promising paradigm for large language models (LLMs) to address real-world challenges. Due to the extensive and irregularly updated number of tools, tool retrieval for selecting the desired tool subset is essential. However, current tool retrieval methods are usually based on academic benchmarks containing overly detailed instructions (e.g., specific API names and parameters), while real-world instructions are more vague. Such a discrepancy would hinder the tool retrieval in real-world applications. In this paper, we first construct a new benchmark, VGToolBench, to simulate human vague instructions. Based on this, we conduct a series of preliminary analyses and find that vague instructions indeed damage the performance of tool retrieval. To this end, we propose a simple-yet-effective Tool Retrieval Bridge (TRB) approach to boost the performance of tool retrieval for vague instructions. The principle of TRB is to introduce a bridge model to rewrite the vague instructions into more specific ones and alleviate the gap between vague instructions and retriever preferences.We conduct extensive experiments under multiple commonly used retrieval settings, and the results show that TRB effectively mitigates the ambiguity of vague instructions while delivering consistent and substantial improvements across all baseline retrievers. For example, with the help of TRB, BM25 achieves a relative improvement of up to 111.51%, i.e., increasing the average NDCG score from 9.73 to 19.59. The source code and models are publicly available at https://github.com/kfchenhn/TRB.

This study presents a comparative analysis of five gender equality certification schemes alongside the ISO 53800 standard with the aim of distilling shared conceptual foundations and design principles that can inform progress toward Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) 5 on gender equality. The comparative analysis reveals marked heterogeneity in scope, design architecture, indicators, and transparency. Methodologically, the study draws on the relevant literature, documentary evidence, and semi-structured consultations with five experts in gender equality, diversity management, auditing, and ESG reporting. Building on the most effective and robust features across gender equality schemes, the study proposes a universal framework for gender equality certification. Under this framework, an ideal universal certification model should apply the same core requirements to both public and private organizations, while including simplified procedures tailored to small- and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs). Moreover, the model should rely on a limited set of key performance indicators (KPIs), focusing on the most material dimensions and prioritizing quantitative measures. It should also strengthen employee feedback mechanisms and enhance accountability in corporate governance. The framework should also pay attention to intersectional dimensions, extend responsibility across the value chain, and address the gender-related implications of artificial intelligence (AI). Importantly, an ideal universal gender equality certification should ensure a high level of transparency through the public disclosure of certified organizations, assessment criteria, KPIs, and levels or scores achieved. Furthermore, it should be supported by a free digital self-assessment tool and robust auditing arrangements, underpinned by a sufficiently large pool of accredited certification bodies and gender-balanced audit teams. Finally, it should undergo periodic review and align with Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) principles and other related SDGs.
